subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Three Laws of Thought
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Three Laws of Thought.

hook.text: Aristotle proposed three laws so fundamental that all rational thought depends on them.

buildup.text: Identity: A is A. A thing is what it is. Sounds obvious, but without it, nothing can be defined.

discovery.text: Non-contradiction: A cannot be both A and not-A at the same time. Something can't be true and false.

twist.text: Excluded middle: A is either true or false — no third option. Quantum physics later challenged this one.

climax.text: These three laws underpin every logical system, every legal code, and every scientific theory.

quiz.question: Which law states something cannot be true and false simultaneously?

details.summary: The three classical laws of thought—identity, non-contradiction, and excluded middle—form the bedrock of Western logic. Every object is identical to itself, nothing can be both true and false, and every statement is either true or false.
details.whyItMatters: These laws underpin all classical reasoning, and challenges to them have generated entirely new logical systems with practical applications.
takeaways: The law of identity states that every object is identical to itself
Non-contradiction: nothing can be A and not-A simultaneously
Excluded middle: every proposition is either true or false

faq.question: Are the three laws of thought universally accepted by all logicians?
faq.answer: No. Intuitionistic logic rejects excluded middle, and paraconsistent logic modifies non-contradiction. These alternatives have applications in computing and quantum logic.

faq.question: Why is the law of non-contradiction considered foundational?
faq.answer: Without it, any statement could be both true and false simultaneously, making all reasoning trivial—everything would follow from everything, and logic would collapse.
